title: eventstream-sendq-throttle-debug-scratchpad
repro_commands: # basic SSE consumer (no buffering): curl -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://api.redwood.example/v1/stream?model=gpt-r1&prompt=hello"

# simulate very slow consumer (throttle stdout with pv): curl -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.redwood.example/v1/stream?model=gpt-r1 | pv -qL 100 > /dev/null
# pause/resume consumer with Node (repro script in ./scripts/pause-consumer.js): node ./scripts/pause-consumer.js
# check socket queues while reproducing: watch -n1 'ss -tnp | grep <server-pid-or-port>'
# capture packets: sudo tcpdump -i any -s0 -w /tmp/sse-backpressure.pcap 'tcp and port 443'
# force network throttling (local dev): sudo tc qdisc add dev lo root tbf rate 100kbit burst 32kbit latency 400ms; # remove with tc qdisc del dev lo root
content:
Notes / breadcrumbs for the intermittent streaming/backpressure bug. Personal scratchpad — very rough.

Summary:
- Observed sessions where server emits SSE chunks fine for ~10s, then client-side recv-Q grows and server starts logging broken pipe / write errors shortly after client resumes. Behavior seems tied to a slow consumer scenario + proxy buffering.
- Repro is intermittent in staging behind envoy/nginx; easier to trigger by intentionally throttling the client (pv / tc / paused reads).

Timeline + symptoms observed:
- 2025-11-09: first reported by support (customer seeing truncated responses after long pauses).
- 2025-11-11: instrumented worker: saw send-Q jump to ~65k for socket while CPU on worker stayed low; server eventually hit EPIPE when trying to write the next chunk and connection went away.
- 2025-12-02: QA reproduced locally by piping to pv -L 50B/s — server wrote ~200 chunks then connection reset.

Local repro notes (what I ran):
- curl -N -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' 'https://api.redwood.example/v1/stream?model=gpt-r1' | pv -qL 100 > /dev/null  # reliable locally
- node scripts/pause-consumer.js -> script opens connection, consumes some chunks, then calls stream.pause() for 12s, then resume; server logs show write blocking and later EPIPE.
- Added 'watch ss -tnp' during run and saw send-Q growing to > 60000 while recv-Q near 0 on server side (i.e. client not ACKing or kernel buffering).

Representative server log snippets:
- 2025-11-11T14:22:10Z WARN [streaming/conn-389] send-Q high=65536 -> applying backpressure to model runner
- 2025-11-11T14:22:24Z ERROR [io/writer] write failed: broken pipe (EPIPE) while streaming delta chunk id=0x7b3c
- 2025-11-11T14:22:24Z DEBUG [runner] last-produced-offset=640128 in-cache; aborted-shard=3

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Proxy or LB buffering combined with client pause -> TCP send buffers fill up then kernel signals RST when buffer pressure grows and server keeps writing. Envoy/nginx config might covertly buffer the stream and hold open connection to downstream.
2) Server doesn't detect slow consumer fast enough (we rely on non-blocking writes and EAGAIN loops); when writes repeatedly return EAGAIN we should apply backpressure to the model runner earlier (we already have a gating mechanism, may be tuned incorrectly).
3) Client or OS-level keepalive/timeouts interfering: some clients close without proper FIN after long pauses, creating RSTs.
4) Memory pressure in connection write path (KV-cache flush causing a large burst followed by no emission -> one big write that fills send-Q).

What I've tried (quick notes):
- Disabled proxy buffering on nginx: set 'proxy_buffering off' and 'X-Accel-Buffering: no' — reduced incidence in one test but not eliminated. Might be a config rollout mismatch.
- Tuned server backpressure thresholds down (send-q threshold from 64k -> 32k) in a sandbox; reproduced still but slightly faster failure (meaning threshold matters but not full fix).
- Added strace -e write -p <pid> while run: observed write() returning -1 EAGAIN repeatedly for ~3s before eventual EPIPE. We probably aren't handling EAGAIN backpressure window long enough.
- Reproduced with and without TLS (terminating at envoy): more flaky when envoy terminates TLS (possibly because envoy has its own buffering/flow control semantics).

Useful debugging commands / low-level checks:
- ss -tnp | grep <port>  # check Send-Q / Recv-Q columns for server socket
- sudo tcpdump -i any -s0 'tcp and port 443' -w /tmp/cap.pcap then open in Wireshark to inspect window updates/zero-window events
- strace -f -e write -p <worker-pid> to see blocking behaviour of userland write syscalls
- sudo perf top / pmap to ensure memory spikes not correlated to the event

Quick repro (full):
1) Start local dev worker (no envoy)
2) run: curl -N -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/stream?model=gpt-r1' | pv -qL 80 > /dev/null
3) observe server logs and ss output

Node pause-consumer.js (notes):
- Implementation: simple https.get(...), on('data') push to buffer, after 5s call stream.pause(), setTimeout(() => stream.resume(), 12000)
- Observed: kernel send-Q jumps and server write returns EAGAIN repeatedly until client resume; on resume client gets only some partial data then TCP connection reset.

Open questions / next actions:
- Is envoy intentionally buffering upstream data for some interval and only flushing in bursts? Check envoy config for 'stream_error_on_invalid_http_message' or 'flush_interval' settings.
- Revisit our non-blocking write loop: do we spin CPU when EAGAIN? should we register POLLOUT and yield model runner earlier? Add metrics for EAGAIN count per connection.
- Add socket-level metrics: send-Q / recv-Q gauge per connection (sample every 1s) and log when > threshold.
- Test with keepalive tweaks: net.ipv4.tcp_retries2, tcp_keepalive_time, and TCP_USER_TIMEOUT to see if an RST path triggers sooner and avoid stuck writes.

Immediate todo for next session:
- Add ephemeral metric for consecutive EAGAINs and expose via console-dashboard for a few days. (Jonah)
- Run end-to-end test with envoy disabled and then with envoy configured 'stream_idle_timeout' low to force earlier reset; compare behavior (Eli).
- Attempt a small runtime change: after N consecutive EAGAINs mark connection as slow and pause model runner output for that connection (Maya).

Notes-to-self:
- This is not the same as chunk boundary corruption — payloads themselves look valid when received. Root cause is flow-control/backpressure.
- Watch for related tickets: RWD-1284 (client-side retry logic) — could be masking issue.

References / past artifacts:
- GH issue: runtime/issues/421 (sse: handle socket backpressure better)
- Linear: RWD-1234 (customer observed truncation)
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime diagnostics (link above)

If I lose this file: also check ~/notes/streaming/sse-backpressure.txt and the test harness in ./scripts.

End of scratchpad.
